stem:
Priya adds one spoon of sugar to a glass of water and stirs until it disappears. The water level drops slightly below the mark she had made on the glass.

Her brother Rohan adds one spoon of sand to another identical glass of water and stirs. The sand settles at the bottom and the water level rises above the mark.

Why do the sugar and the sand affect the water level differently?

options.text: Sugar particles fit into the spaces between water particles, but sand particles do not dissolve and take up space themselves.
All small solids behave in the same way when stirred into water, so the levels should be identical.
Sugar particles push the water particles apart, while sand particles fit into the spaces between water particles.
Sugar is heavier than sand, so it pulls the water level down, while sand floats and pushes the level up.

teacher.key_rationale: Dissolved sugar particles occupy the interparticle spaces between water particles, so the level may fall slightly; insoluble sand settles and occupies space, raising the total level. Option A states this correctly. B is the blanket-scope misconception, C reverses the relationship, and D gives a false density/floatation explanation.
